fixes.explanation: Careful, friend, because Paul says it bigger than that. He says Phoebe "…has been a great help to many people, including me." Look at that little word "many." Paul is one of a whole line of folks she has helped.

You got it, baker. Paul says to watch out for those who create divisions and obstacles contrary to the teaching they have learned, and then he adds, "Turn away from them." It's short and it's plain. No long speech needed, and I'm the one with a mustache to spare.

That sounds like a lot of work, friend, and Paul never asks for it. His instruction is just four words: "Turn away from them." He says it about those who create divisions and obstacles contrary to the teaching the believers had learned. A public debate isn't in the verse at all.

Yes, baker. Paul says such people "…are not serving our Lord Christ, but their own appetites." Their hearts are pointed at what they want instead of at Christ. That's a serious thing, and Paul says it plainly.

Not quite, friend. Paul never mentions loud threats. He says that "By smooth talk and flattery they deceive the hearts of the naive." The fooling comes through smooth talk and flattery, so it's worth being careful with sweet-sounding words.

That's it, baker. Paul says, "But I want you to be wise about what is good and innocent about what is evil." So he wants them wise about the good and innocent about the evil. Know the good well, and keep clear of the evil.

That's him, baker. Tertius says it himself: "I, Tertius, who wrote down this letter, greet you in the Lord." When he writes "I," it's his own voice breaking into Paul's letter. I think it's a nice touch that the one holding the pen gets to say hello.

That's a bit off, baker. The text never calls Tertius a leader of the church in Rome. He says, "I, Tertius, who wrote down this letter, greet you in the Lord." What he tells us about himself is that he wrote the letter down.
You got it, baker. Paul says Gaius "…has hosted me and all the church…" That's Paul and the whole church that Gaius hosted. I can barely handle a few bakers crowding my counter, so I'm impressed.
Yes, baker. Paul says the mystery is made known "…in order to lead all nations to the obedience that comes from faith…" Not just one nation, but all of them. That's a wide reach for a message.

Good thinking, baker, but it isn't Paul's answer. He ends with, "…to the only wise God be glory forever through Jesus Christ! Amen." It's Jesus Christ he names. So the apostles don't make it into that final line.
